top.title: A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut
top.summary: Scientists have discovered that fasting for just 24 hours increases a beneficial gut bacterium that helps the intestines regenerate after radiation damage. The preclinical findings could pave the way for new treatments that protect healthy tissue during cancer therapy, potentially without requiring patients to fast.
top.text: A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms. The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine. "Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more quickly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness plan," Piwnica-Worms said. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response." Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure. When this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options. Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory showed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect. The latest study provides an important piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury. Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila , also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage. Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence. These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant. In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining. To determine how important AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits. Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study. The results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs. By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment. Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy. One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage. If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy. Importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care. "Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai said. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need." top.title: MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body
top.summary: MIT scientists have developed nanoparticles that reprogram immune cells directly inside the body to attack cancer and harmful immune cells, eliminating tumors and reversing liver damage in mouse experiments. The breakthrough could make powerful immune therapies dramatically simpler and less expensive while opening new possibilities for treating cancer and autoimmune diseases.
top.text: MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer. The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis. Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells. The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies. "The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science. Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology . The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study. Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker. CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma. However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient. Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells. Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment. Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other. "NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says. Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body. "If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says. Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval. The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target. The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks. To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed. Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target. The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice. The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting. They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission. The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans. In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated. Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals. This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies. The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues. They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response. The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed. These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment. "This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says. top.title: Liver transplant linked to significantly extended survival for alcohol-associated disease yet access is not equitable
top.summary: People with alcohol-associated liver disease who received a liver transplant survived years longer than those who did not, but there are disparities in which patients receive a transplant. A large study published in Alcohol: Clinical and Experimental Research found that liver transplantation was associated with significantly longer survival in both the short term and longer term. Yet, women and African Americans had lower odds of receiving a transplant, even though neither group had a higher risk of death than men or white patients.

top.title: Community CPR and EMS intervention program did not increase survival after cardiac arrest
top.summary: A comprehensive emergency medical services and community-based educational intervention in North Carolina focused on recognizing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and actions needed quickly to increase bystander CPR and use of an automated external defibrillator (AED) did not significantly improve patient survival with favorable brain function, according to new, independent, preliminary, late-breaking science presented Sunday at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions in Chicago.

top.title: How a protein contributes to blood vessel damage in the brain in patients with malaria
top.summary: Malaria remains one of the deadliest infectious diseases worldwide. According to World Health Organization (WHO) estimates, there were more than 280 million cases in 2024, with 610,000 people dying from the parasitic infection. Ninety-five percent of deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, where children under the age of 5 are particularly affected. Prompt treatment is crucial. Nevertheless, some patients die from malaria even when treated with medication.

top.title: GLP-1 drugs show lower obesity-related cancer risk than insulin, but not all diabetes treatments
top.summary: Years of research point to obesity and type 2 diabetes raising the risk of developing several types of cancer. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a recent medical breakthrough, were originally developed for blood sugar control or diabetes management and also work overtime promoting weight loss. Scientists are curious to explore whether there are any links between these drugs and the onset of cancers in people with diabetes.

top.title: Rare eye condition prompts new FDA warning on popular GLP-1 drugs
top.summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is requiring makers of Ozempic, Wegovy and similar drugs to warn of a rare eye condition that can cause vision loss.

top.title: Even substitute PFAS cause metabolic stress in zebrafish embryos
top.summary: Publishing in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances, researchers from Kyushu University used zebrafish embryos to study the health effects of the PFAS called PFBS (perfluorobutanesulfonic acid), a substitute PFAS thought to be safer than traditional compounds. They found that while PFBS did not generate any obvious external dysfunction, the compound still gets absorbed and accumulates in the zebrafish embryo. Results showed that PFBS caused disruptions in the metabolic pathways for sugars and fat, which led to oxidative stress. Embryos also showed physical impairments in heart function, facial development, nervous system development and visual response.

top.title: New clinical definition of obesity could help target care more effectively, saving time and money
top.summary: The traditional way of assessing whether someone is overweight using body mass index (BMI) may fail to capture whether excess body fat is harmful and could be supplemented with a second measure when assessing patients, a new UCL study suggests.

top.title: Psychedelic aftereffects may offer a window into psychotic symptoms
top.summary: Every night, as he fell asleep, a 25-year-old man saw an eye in his ceiling. It was huge and unblinking, and it felt as if the whole world was being sucked into it. He didn't have psychosis, and he wasn't on drugs. But he had taken psychedelics in the past, and he was worried enough to contact Max Greenwald, an M.D.-Ph.D. student at Yale School of Medicine, with a question: Was he developing psychosis?

top.title: Scientists identify protein driving age-related organ damage
top.summary: Monash University researchers have identified a protein that drives age-related damage in vital organs, opening a potential new avenue for treatments that could help people stay healthier as they get older. Published in Immunity, the research revealed a link between the protein granzyme K and signs of aging in the heart, liver and kidneys.

top.title: Precision RNA therapy offers hope for brain receptor disorders
top.summary: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and Academia Sinica in Taiwan have developed an experimental RNA-based treatment that prevents brain damage and improves learning, memory and social behavior in mice carrying a rare genetic mutation associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.

top.title: Researchers trial AI coach for diabetes
top.summary: For many people with type 2 diabetes, the challenge isn't understanding what they need to do to stay well. It's doing it consistently. Managing the condition often requires a long-term commitment to healthier eating patterns, regular exercise and medication. But unlike some illnesses, diabetes can progress quietly. Missing a dose or skipping exercise may not cause immediate consequences, making it easy for healthy intentions to slip amid the demands of work, family and everyday life.

top.title: Predator-like scent activates an anxiety-related brain circuit in mice
top.summary: Anxiety disorders are some of the most common psychiatric conditions, estimated to affect around 4.4% of people worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. While neuroscientists have been studying these disorders for decades, their neural underpinnings are not yet fully understood.

top.title: Asteroid mining will crash the platinum market, but that's good news for Earth
top.summary: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question—what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

top.title: A lingering blue glow and unexpected energy levels hint at new ways to control light in advanced materials
top.summary: Scientists from the Physics Department and Organic Electroactive Materials research group at Durham University have made significant advances in understanding how materials absorb and release light in two recently published research papers in Nature Communications.

top.title: Pumpkin seed protein puts a twist on nondairy coffee creamer
top.summary: Pumpkin season is about more than cute décor. The squash contains lots of seeds with a high protein content, but they're usually discarded. Researchers reporting in ACS' Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry found another way to use the seeds, extracting that protein to create a plant-based coffee creamer. In initial taste tests, participants preferred the new creamer to a commercial nondairy option because it preserved the flavor and aroma of coffee better.

top.title: Sequential peaks in arthropod availability across snow and vegetation help sustain alpine birds
top.summary: The alpine zone is located above the tree line in mountainous regions and is characterized by long winters and short growing seasons. Birds and other animals inhabiting these environments breed during a limited period extending from spring to summer. Arthropods, including insects and spiders, serve as an essential food resource during this time.

top.title: Sensors track stress in plants in real time—without hurting them in the process
top.summary: Even plants, from towering palm trees to vegetables such as onions and eggplants, can get stressed. Now, a team of engineers has designed a new kind of sensor that attaches directly to plants and peers inside them to track how they respond to stressors such as drought and fires in real time.

top.title: How populist leaders dismantle intelligence agencies from within: New study reveals the 'intelligence cyclone'
top.summary: A new joint study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) and The Hebrew University of Jerusalem reveals how populist leaderships systematically undermine, discredit and ultimately capture intelligence agencies, transforming vital national security bodies into political echo chambers. The research, published in Contemporary Security Policy, warns that when populist politicians treat secret services as "deep state" adversaries, they disrupt objective threat analysis and leave democracies blind to catastrophic surprise attacks.

top.title: How Chinese brewers refined their booze 5,000 years ago
top.summary: More than 5,000 years ago, brewers in eastern China appear to have used red mold to make rice alcohol, then strained the drink through cloth. Microscopic residues on ancient pottery show evidence of both the fermentation method and the filtering process to separate the liquid from leftover grain.

top.title: Happy face, angry voice: Human–dog interaction study tracks conflicting cues
top.summary: Dogs, having lived alongside humans for tens of thousands of years, are keenly tuned in to our emotions. Behavioral experiments, brain studies and even measurements of heart rate all suggest dogs respond differently depending on the emotional expressions they encounter in humans.

top.title: A newly discovered South African dinosaur was a heavyweight even as a youngster
top.summary: It probably walked on two legs and weighed about 400 kilograms (880 pounds), despite still being a youngster. Meet Nyana rooiwalensis, a newly identified dinosaur species that lived more than 200 million years ago in what is now South Africa.

top.title: Milk and wine used in Menorcan funerary rituals over 2,000 years ago
top.summary: In the Late Iron Age, or post-Talayotic period, over 2,000 years ago, Menorca and the other Balearic Islands experienced increasing connectivity with the wider Mediterranean. However, they also maintained distinctive local funerary traditions, such as burying their loved ones in rock-cut tombs, or artificial caves. Some of these caves contained external courtyards located in front of the burial chambers where animal offerings might have been made. Archaeologists even suspect that perishable foods or liquids were offered in characteristic island containers, such as high-bottomed vessels. Until now, however, the contents of these ceramic containers had never been identified.

top.title: Archaeologists uncover a witness to the Neolithic revolution
top.summary: Radiocarbon dating and isotope analysis of an immaculately preserved skeleton from Mesolithic Denmark indicate that the individual lived through the introduction of agriculture and adapted his diet to the change, providing a unique "eyewitness account" of one of humanity's most significant technological revolutions.

top.title: Heavy rain can more than double glacier speeds in Alaska
top.summary: Glaciers are often thought of as unyielding blocks of ice that slowly carve out the landscape as they move downhill by gravity. But sometimes their slow crawl becomes a surge that sees them move orders of magnitude faster than their usual speed.

top.title: Why do farts smell so bad? A microbiologist explains the odors brewing in your gut
top.summary: Your farts’ aromas are tuned to your diet – and your overall health.
top.text: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com . Why do farts smell so bad? – Daisy, age 7, New York, New York A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day . All together, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon. Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut . These organisms have an important job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts. As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria , called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health . Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping. So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink? Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe . Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid. But wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur . Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek. One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide , which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol , which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide , which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood. Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts. The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat . Some types of foods often referred to as junk food , including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder . However, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch . Food is a key source of amino acids , nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains . Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them . When you eat sulfur-rich foods , your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases . That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health . In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness , such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about. As you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates , including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise. Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia . According to the Guinness book of world records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts . The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “ Despicable Me ,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mis-hears his boss’s demand for a dart gun , instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy. But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand , spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances , such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself . Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules. These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves and volcano vents that can suffocate and kill you . So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect. top.title: GLP-1 drugs carry risk of rare but serious eye condition – a physician studying these medicines explains the potential side effect
top.summary: Doctors often call the condition a stroke of the eye – and though the risk is small, patients should know the symptoms and seek immediate treatment if they occur.
top.text: GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a potential link to a rare eye condition that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on Nov. 9. 2026. The eye condition is called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy , or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a stroke of the eye. I am a clinician and epidemiologist who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION . Millions of people around the world take these medications – including 30 million in the U.S. – to treat diabetes and obesity and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are also being investigated for an expanding list of clinical conditions . The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so. Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect. NAION is an injury to the optic nerve , which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow. Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness. These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment. Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower. As use of GLP-1 drugs increased – particularly since 2021, when they were approved for obesity – cases of NAION began to emerge. A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link. It reported an increased risk of the eye condition among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug. To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the FDA first compiled data from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs. Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients – 78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison. Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug. This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs. In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of sentinel programs that track the real-world safety of approved medications. They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024. Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1. Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000. This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs. Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION . For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly 600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years. For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication. In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients. That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients. For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk. What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes. It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this. The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide. It concluded that this eye condition is a very rare side effect of semaglutide and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect. The risk of NAION with GLP-1 drugs is likely real. All the evidence – the FDA’s two analyses, the real-world studies conducted by independent researchers and the fact that two regulators reached the same view independently – points in the same direction. But in terms of the total number of people who are likely to experience this side effect, the risk is small. In my view, this makes the FDA’s warning not a cause for alarm but rather an unlikely but not impossible outcome that both clinicians and patients should be aware of. Clinicians should discuss it with their patients before prescribing a GLP-1 drug – and patients should be educated on the symptoms of NAION and how to tell if they are experiencing it. Patients should also seek immediate care at the earliest signs of vision problems. For patients who have previously had NAION or who already have risk factors for it , including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia and kidney disease, careful discussion weighing the risks and benefits is important.

top.title: You likely have genes that affect how well your medications work – testing for them could improve treatment
top.summary: Researchers found that everyone in a 100,000 sample of people has at least one genetic variant that interacts with common prescriptions.
top.text: All people carry differences in their DNA that could affect how they respond to medication , according to my team’s newly published research. Moreover, 1 in 4 already take a medication their body processes differently because of their genetics. Clinicians often take a trial and error approach to prescriptions. Two people take the same medicine at the same dose. One starts feeling better, but the other experiences side effects or sees little benefit. For some medications, part of the reason behind that difference in response is written in a person’s DNA. The field of pharmacogenomics studies how variations in your DNA contribute to how your body processes and responds to medicines. For instance, genes can influence how quickly your liver breaks down a drug and how long it stays in your bloodstream. But using genetic testing to guide prescriptions is not yet routine. Part of the problem is a lack of large population data to study this approach more broadly. Clinicians don’t know when it’s best to order genetic testing. And because most genetic research has been done on people of European ancestry , researchers know less about how common key gene variants are in everyone else. To improve the diversity of pharmacogenomic data, my team of researchers and I analyzed the whole genome sequences and health records of nearly 100,000 participants in the All of Us Research Program . All of Us is an effort from the National Institutes of Health to study the health of 1 million or more people across the U.S. and its territories, with a focus on groups historically left out of biomedical research. We examined 16 genes with well-established links to how someone responds to different medications, pairing this data with electronic health records to identify which drugs participants had already taken. We found that every participant carried at least one relevant genetic variant , and many carried several. Around 99.5% of participants had a genetic variant for which the Food and Drug Administration or medical guidelines recommend a different drug or change in dose for certain medications. Even more telling, about 24% had taken a drug that is affected by a genetic variant they carried. Common examples included drugs used to reduce excess stomach acid, such as omeprazole and pantoprazole, and statins used to lower cholesterol levels. Because health records can be incomplete, our results likely underestimate the actual prevalence of these gene-drug interactions. These findings can help improve the databases clinicians and researchers use routinely in research. We identified 17,704 previously unreported variants in the regions of these genes that encode proteins. Computer models predicted that about a quarter may have significant effects on how the body processes drugs. Our team also reported the frequencies of hundreds of genetic variants linked to drug response for people from genetic ancestries that previously had incomplete data. Overall, our research shows that DNA variation is very common, and broader genetic testing may help optimize the medications clinicians prescribe to patients. It’s also an example of how big initiatives such as the All of Us Research Program can advance precision medicine . However, this study doesn’t prove testing would improve outcomes for each of these people. Additionally, genes are only one factor; age, kidney and liver function, and other medications also affect how the body processes drugs . Still, I believe the direction of the research is clear. Pharmacogenomics can provide potentially relevant benefits for many people who take medications.

top.title: What is ‘food is medicine?’ – 2 experts explain this decades-old approach to healthcare that is taking on new life
top.summary: Food is medicine aims to help patients prevent or manage chronic illnesses by eating food that supports their health.
top.text: Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health . Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes , heart disease and high blood pressure . This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions . Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness. As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community. Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs. Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household. Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million . Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health. Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement , U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “ Eat Real Food .” But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger . In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta. When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.” Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members. In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually . Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance . This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs. Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local. One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight , waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants. For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers . One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods. One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security . Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels . This data supports our own previous findings. However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week , which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes. Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries. Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
